newsitem.title: USA: Perot vows to stay in U.S. presidential race.
newsitem.headline: Perot vows to stay in U.S. presidential race.

text.p: Reform Party candidate Ross Perot, excluded from the head-to-head U.S. presidential television debates, vowed on Sunday to stay in the race to the finish and urged voters to vote with their conscience.

During a television interview the Texas billionaire also blasted Republican candidate Bob Dole's promise of a 15 percent tax cut as a candy handout that echoed President Ronald Reagan's unworkable 1980s "voodoo economics."

Perot, stuck in third place in the polls with less than 5 percent, was attempting to make his presence felt with a series of television interviews as President Bill Clinton and Dole prepared for their first debate on Sunday. A post-debate appearance was scheduled on CNN's "Larry King Show."

He also appeared on ABC-TV in a paid 30-minute advertisement at 7 p.m. EDT (2300 GMT)-- just two hours before the presidential debate -- and said neither Democrats nor Republicans wanted him in the debate because he was raising issues they wanted to ignore, including the ballooning costs of Medicare, Medicaid and Social Security.

"In business you promote people based on their performance. In politics people get promoted on their acting ability and their appearance, and the bad news is they go on acting after the election instead of going to work and producing results for the people," Perot said.

He urged voters disgruntled with the two mainstream parties to vote for him Nov. 5. "Vote for the Reform Party in 1996, then they won't be able to push you around in 2000. You'll be in the debate," he said, in one of many direct jabs at the debate organizers for excluding him.
Perot appealed to voters not to ignore him simply because the Democrats and Republicans were saying he could not win.
Perot cited exit polls in the 1992 election which showed 40 percent of voters would have chosen Perot if they had voted their conscience, 31 percent Clinton and 27 percent Bush.
"The future of this country is in the hands of the people if they would just grasp it. They have got to vote their consciences," Perot said during CBS Television's "Face The Nation" program.

"We will be in this race to the end because I want the American people to be able to vote their conscience. I hope they don't get talked out of it like they did last time when they were told don't vote for Perot, he can't win.
"That's the whole game because the people say they want to vote for a winner. You've got to vote for someone who will face and deal with our country's problems."
A trailer on Perot's informercial promised people who made a donation to the Reform Party a free copy of Perot's book, "Ross Perot: My Life and the Secrets of My Success."
A federal appeals court on Friday rejected a last-ditch emergency appeal by Perot and another presidential candidate with low support to try to get included in the debate.
Perot criticized Dole's promises of an across-the-board tax cut if elected.

"When we can't pay our bills, only in America after the biggest tax increase in history a couple years ago would we offer the American people a tax cut. One or the other can't make any sense. But the whole game is to give people free candy just before an election," said Perot.
"The theory is supply side or trickle-down economics. We tried that during the Reagan years and we had the largest increase in the debt in the history of our country," he said.
"A huge part of our total debt came as a result of that that sort of thinking. It didn't work. It was later called voodoo economics and now it's back again in 1996."
